answer: The issue is that untrained random weights produce extreme Z2 values. After subtracting max(Z2), some exponents are still too negative, causing numerical underflow. Most values become ~0, and division creates floating-point errors. Initialize weights using proper schemes (e.g., Xavier initialization): `W1 = np.random.randn(784, 10) * 0.01` and `W2 = np.random.randn(10, 10) * 0.01`. Alternatively, clamp Z2 to prevent extreme values: `Z2 = np.clip(Z2, -500, 500)` before softmax. The softmax axis logic is correct with `axis=0, keepdims=True`; the real problem is activation saturation from random initialization.

In NumPy, `True` and `False` are treated as integers 1 and 0. So `matrix[True, False]` is equivalent to `matrix[1, 0]`—the element at row 1, column 0. `matrix[True, True]` becomes `matrix[1, 1]`. Compare this to `matrix[[True, False]]` which uses a list for boolean indexing (selecting rows where the condition is True). Use list syntax for boolean indexing: `matrix[[True, False]]` selects rows. Use scalar indices for positional access: `matrix[0, 1]` or `matrix[True, False]` (as positional 1, 0).

By default, `asyncio.gather()` doesn't cancel pending tasks when one fails—it collects all results/exceptions. To auto-cancel others on failure, use Python 3.11+ `asyncio.TaskGroup`: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: tg.create_task(worker(i)) for i in range(5)`. For older Python, manually cancel remaining tasks: `tasks = [asyncio.create_task(worker(i)) for i in range(5)]; try: await asyncio.gather(*tasks) except Exception: [t.cancel() for t in tasks]`. Or pass `return_exceptions=True` to gather and filter exceptions yourself.

gTTS and edge-tts require internet; pyttsx3/piper-tts need system libraries. For Render deployment, use `piper-tts` (offline, self-contained): install via `pip install piper-tts`. It requires no external APIs. For MP3 output, pipe Piper to FFmpeg: `ffmpeg -i input.wav output.mp3`. Alternatively, use AWS Polly with local caching: download MP3s once, serve from cache. For 3000-word texts, split into chunks to avoid timeouts. Test locally with your Render environment first—install required system libs in Dockerfile.

Use Polars' `explode()` instead of converting to Python lists: `unique_vals = df.select([pl.col('a'), pl.col('b')]).unpivot().unnest('value').select(pl.col('value').explode().unique())`. Or simpler: `df.with_columns([pl.col('a').explode(), pl.col('b').explode()]).select(pl.concat_list(['a', 'b']).list.explode().unique())`. Best approach: `pl.concat([df['a'], df['b']]).explode().unique()`. This avoids `to_list()` overhead and keeps computation in Polars' optimized engine.

VS Code's terminal doesn't render ANSI color codes by default. Enable them in VS Code settings: open settings.json and add `"terminal.integrated.env.windows": {"FORCE_COLOR": "1"}` or check `Ctrl+Shift+P` > Terminal: Run Recent Command > toggle color support. Alternatively, Jupyter notebooks render ANSI colors better. For terminal output, pipe to `less -R` (preserves colors). Note: ANSI 256-color sequences work; true RGB (24-bit) support varies by terminal.

Your `starttime` approach is sound for detecting PID reuse, but inode is more reliable. Get inode: `os.stat(f'/proc/{pid}', dir_fd=None).st_ino`. If inode differs, PID reused. Alternatively, compare `ino` field from `/proc/[pid]/stat` directly. For modern Linux, use `pidfd_open()` (available in Python 3.10+): `os.pidfd_open(pid)`. Then check if process still alive: `os.waitid(os.P_PIDFD, pidfd, os.WNOHANG | os.WNOWAIT)`. This avoids parsing `/proc/` and handles rollover safely.

Plotly treemaps show hierarchy with nested boxes. To display only leaf-level squares with parent color as legend: 1) Don't include root in `path`—use `path=['product', 'city']` instead. 2) Customize parent display: `fig.update_layout(treemapcolorcolors='colors_list')` and hide parent labels. 3) Or use `plotly.graph_objects` for finer control. For the exact layout you want, consider `squarify` + `matplotlib` with manual coloring by parent: color each product differently, then draw city squares within.

Multiprocessing/Joblib fork data—modifications don't persist to parent. Solutions: 1) Return modified values: `result = Pool.starmap(Test, data); a = result`. 2) Use shared memory: `arr = multiprocessing.Array('B', 10); Pool.starmap(Test, [(i, arr, 10) for i in range(2)])`. 3) Use `multiprocessing.Manager().list()` for shared state. 4) Use `joblib.Parallel(backend='threading')` for in-process parallelism (no GIL for I/O). Recommend option 1—pure functions are cleaner and avoid synchronization bugs.

py3dep fetches one patch at a time. Optimize: 1) Batch requests—download multiple DEMs in one call if the library supports it. 2) Parallelize with `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` or `asyncio` to fetch multiple patches concurrently. 3) Cache downloaded DEMs to avoid re-fetching. 4) Use `rasterio.open()` to check if DEM already exists locally. 5) Consider alternative sources: USGS 3DEP via AWS S3 (faster bulk downloads) or Google Earth Engine. 60 hours suggests sequential fetching—parallelizing should reduce it to <6 hours.

The error occurs because Alembic tries to compare your in-memory schema against a target database during migration generation. For multi-tenant migrations: 1) Use a `--sql` mode to generate DDL without connecting. 2) Create a reference 'template' database schema locally (not in-memory) to compare against. 3) Use `compare_type=True, compare_server_default=True` on a real database connection. 4) Or: generate migrations manually without auto-detection: `alembic revision --message 'description'` and write SQL/ORM operations by hand. Store template schema in git for consistency.

Use nested list comprehension: `mapped = [(row, col) for row, cols in zip(rows, cols) for col in cols]`. This zips rows with cols, then for each pair, creates tuples of (row, col_element) for every element in cols[i]. Result: `[(502, 555), (502, 905), (1064, 155), ...]`. Alternatively with itertools: `from itertools import chain, repeat; mapped = [(r, c) for r, cs in zip(rows, cols) for c in cs]` (same logic). Nested loops are most readable here.

Issues merging depth maps: 1) Verify rotation matrices are correct (use `scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation`). 2) Align coordinate systems—ensure Z-axis is consistent across rotations. 3) Use point cloud registration (ICP algorithm): `open3d.pipelines.registration.registration_icp()` to auto-align overlapping regions. 4) Merge via voxel grid or TSDF fusion for robust blending. Recommend Open3D library: `pcd = o3d.geometry.PointCloud(); pcd.points = o3d.utility.Vector3dVector(xyz); o3d.io.write_point_cloud('output.ply', pcd)`.

`np.vectorize()` calls your function twice: once to infer output type/dtype (with a sample element) and again for actual computation. To reduce overhead, pass `otypes=[np.str_]` to skip type detection: `np.vectorize(f, otypes=[np.str_])(['input'])`. For better performance, avoid vectorize—use list comprehensions or apply. If you need vectorization, consider `numba.jit` or `numexpr` for numeric operations. Vectorize is convenient but slow; it's a wrapper around Python loops, not true vectorization.

Regex alone won't work reliably (// in URLs breaks it). Solution: 1) Parse JSONC properly using `json5` or `jsoncomment` libraries. 2) If regex-only required, split JSON strings first (find quoted strings, protect them), remove comments, then re-join. 3) Fallback regex that handles strings: `r'(?:"[^"]*"|//[^\n]*)'` with grouping to preserve strings. Better: use a proper JSONC parser: `pip install json5; json5.loads(jsonc_str)`. Regex for comments is fragile; parsers handle edge cases.

After thresholding, extract root length: 1) Skeletonize the binary mask: `from skimage.morphology import skeletonize; skeleton = skeletonize(cleaned_mask)`. 2) Count skeleton pixels (length proxy) or fit line to skeleton points. 3) Use PlantCV: `analyzed = pcv.analyze_object(img, mask)` which computes object dimensions. 4) For precise root length, use medial axis transform (`skimage.ndimage.distance_transform_edt`) and trace longest path. 5) Or use `PlantCV.Segment` tools on mask to identify individual roots, then measure each.

QGIS loads plugins at startup; runtime installation needs manual reload. Use `qgis.utils.reload_plugin('plugin_name')` or iterate through active plugins: `from qgis.utils import active_plugins; active_plugins.append('tools')` and reload. Better: after extracting plugin ZIP, call `iface.mainWindow().blockSignals(False); qgis.utils.plugins['tools'].initGui()` to trigger GUI setup. Or restart QGIS via subprocess call. For user-friendly flow, either trigger restart or show message: 'Plugin installed; please restart QGIS'.

OR-Tools doesn't directly support difference constraints on cumul dimensions. Workaround: 1) Add a custom dimension for ride time: create a separate 'ride_time' dimension tracking (current_cumul - pickup_cumul). 2) Use slack variables: for each customer, add auxiliary variable `slack_i = end_cumul - pickup_cumul`, set upper bound `slack_i <= 60`, add penalty `solver.AddDisjunctiveConstraint([...], coeff=1)` for violations. 3) Or: solve in two phases—first assign customers to routes, then check feasibility. 4) Simplest: use `AddDimension` with custom callback evaluating ride time per customer.

Use `pandas.value_counts()` (already doing this—it's efficient). To optimize further: 1) Use `pd.Series.value_counts(sort=False)` to skip sorting if order doesn't matter. 2) Cache results: `cache = {q: values[q].value_counts().to_dict() for q in questions}`. 3) For bulk processing, use `groupby` + `agg` instead of looping: `data.groupby('Q1').size()`. 4) Pre-filter: `data[data['Q1'].notna()].value_counts()` to exclude NaN. Current approach is already O(n log n)—optimization gains are minimal unless data is massive (>>1M rows). Focus on matplotlib rendering speed instead.
